question: A browser parser encounters `<br clear="left">`. Why does this fail to clear in modern HTML?
options: the clear attribute is deprecated and deprecated attributes are ignored
br is a void element and cannot accept non-boolean attributes
html5 deprecated clear in favor of css floats
the value left is invalid for non-block elements
explanation: HTML5 removed the clear attribute as a presentation concern; clearing floats is now purely a CSS responsibility.

question: A form field is defined as `<input name='password' disabled>`. Which statement is true about form submission?
options: the field is submitted with an empty string value
the field is omitted from submission entirely
the field is submitted with the name attribute only
submission is prevented by the disabled attribute
explanation: Disabled form controls are excluded from form submission regardless of whether they have a value.

question: Given `<meta charset="UTF-8">` placed after `<title>`, a page displays mojibake (garbled characters). What is the root cause?
options: utf-8 encoding is incompatible with the title element
charset meta must appear before any content including title
the server sent an incorrect content-type header
the browser has cached incorrect encoding detection
explanation: The charset meta tag must appear in the first 1024 bytes of the document head before any content to ensure the parser uses correct encoding from the start.

question: Why does `<input type='email' value='test@example.com' readonly>` differ from `<input type='email' value='test@example.com' disabled>`?
options: readonly still allows javascript to modify the value, disabled does not
readonly is submitted in forms, disabled is excluded
readonly allows keyboard focus, disabled does not
readonly appears as editable to screen readers, disabled does not
explanation: Readonly fields are included in form submission (readonly data is sent), but disabled fields are completely excluded.

question:
A single page has `

Product

` twice and uses entity-encoded `<h2>Subtitle</h2>` for display. Which breaks accessibility?
options: entity-encoded tags are parsed as text and assistive tech sees them
two h1 elements confuse screen readers into skipping the second one
entities are always parsed visually so markup intent is lost
headings encoded as entities bypass outline algorithms
explanation: Entity-encoded HTML markup (`<h1>`) is rendered as literal text, not parsed as an element, so it is invisible to accessibility tree algorithms and SEO parsers.

question: An SVG is embedded as `<svg><defs><style>circle{fill:red}</style></defs><circle cx='50' cy='50' r='40'/></svg>`. The circle appears green, not red. Why?
options: svg does not support inline styles inside defs
the circle element is defined before the style rule applies
external css is overriding the embedded style
svgs require xlink namespace for style application
explanation: External CSS rules (from the page's stylesheets) have higher specificity than styles defined inside SVG `<defs>`, so page-level styles override embedded SVG styles.

question: Which void element must NOT have a closing tag in HTML5?
options: img
br
hr
all of the above are valid void elements
explanation: All three (img, br, hr) are void elements in HTML5; they never have closing tags and never wrap content.

question: A developer writes `<div data-count='5'>` and later reads `element.getAttribute('data-count')` returning `'5'`, but `element.dataset.count` returns `5`. Which statement is true?
options: getattribute returns a number, dataset returns a string
dataset auto-converts numeric strings to numbers
getattribute reads the raw html, dataset applies type coercion
this is browser-dependent and will fail in some environments
explanation: getAttribute() returns the raw HTML string value; the dataset API parses data-* attributes and may coerce types, but both ultimately return strings in conformant implementations.

question: An HTML5 document has `<!DOCTYPE html>` but the page serves as `application/xhtml+xml`. Which parsing mode activates?
options: html5 mode because doctype always determines parsing
xhtml strict mode because content-type overrides doctype
html5 mode unless the content-type is explicitly set
parser defaults to quirks mode due to conflicting signals
explanation: When the Content-Type header explicitly specifies `application/xhtml+xml`, the browser uses XML parsing mode regardless of the HTML5 DOCTYPE, requiring valid XML structure.

question: Why might `<a href='#section' id='section'>` create a navigation loop issue on some browsers?
options: the id matches the href, causing infinite history entries when clicked
anchor ids must be unique, and href references create duplicate ids
browsers treat self-referential anchors as page reloads
focus management directs to the element, then immediately back to the link
explanation: Clicking an anchor that links to itself can cause browsers to add redundant history entries or create navigation loops in some implementations.
